Twelve full-page suffrage miniatures, framed and on tooled gold or diapered pink and blue ground, in pairs at alternating openings before the Calendar. Their style is associated with the Queen Mary Psalter workshop ( ). The same artist worked on a Psalter made for a patron in the Norwich diocese, which later passed to Peterborough Abbey (London, British Library, Royal MS 2.B.vii ). Cambridge, Corpus Christi College, MS 53 1v: woman (perhaps intended to represent the commissioner or an early owner of the manuscript) kneeling in veneration before a sainted archbishop. The archbishop (?St Thomas, ?St Edmund) was altered from being a bishop (perhaps originally St Hugh, as in the Calendar) by the substitution of a cross for a crozier and the addition of a pallium. Plain initials, in the same ink as the text, outlined by dots of red. At chapter divisions, these occupy the blank space above and below the written line (e.g. ff. 131v, 169v, 174r, 177r, 179r) . At verse divisions, they are slightly larger than the written line.

Larger, more decorative handwriting with otiose strokes and additional flourishes is adopted for the titles of the two saints’ lives ( and ) and far more significantly in the case of the Lydgate. The scribe also shows a greater preponderance for otiose strokes in the verse. Underlining of occasional passages throughout.

The volume is very copiously illustrated, and in a very curious way. There are two sets of pictures : the one illustrates the text, the other consists of a series of full-page pictures (in nearly all cases) which are appropriate only to a religious book, and as I take it, must be copied from a Psalter. Psalters usually had a series of preliminary paintings illustrating the Life of Christ, and the principal Saints. All these pictures are by the same hand. They are extremely roughly drawn and coloured, almost no gold is used. The originals were probably very fine.

There are at the beginning of the book some admirable decorative initials in gold and colours. These have a green edging. They should be compared with two MSS. at Trinity College, B.5.3 and O.5.8. Within it is Moses, with red nimbus, white beard, pink mantle over white, kneeling. On R. in green medallion a bust of Christ with red nimbus holding a scroll which has been inscribed in cent. xv. Folio 1v features a full-page miniature which shows a man in a wooden pulpit wearing a scarlet cloth addressing a group of seated and standing men and women. This group includes a prince in a gold robe and a lady in diadem against a background of hills and trees. In the right corner of the background there is a pink-coloured turreted castle with a group of people in front of it: this group shows a crowned queen in blue over white and a (?) wreathed king in red in front of it. Before them a prince kneels presenting a gold cap or crown. In the left background and further away, there is dark castle on a rock from which a grop of brightly clad figures descends. The miniature is painted on a gold ground and surmoun5ed by a full border of acanthus leaves in scarlet, blue and pink on a gold ground with extending tendrils, gold besants and coloured leaves. Many interpretations of this frontispiece exist but scholars generally agree that the man in the pulpit is Geoffrey Chaucer and that the man in gold brocade who immediately stands before him is Richard II (1367-1400) [although others have suggested that he is a later English king or Charles d'Orleans]. For further discussion of the miniature and possible identification of the members in the audience see e.g. Brusendorff (1925); Galway (1949); Williams (1962); Kendrick (1987); Lerer (1993); Scott (1996); Helmbold (2008); Coleman (2010); Helmbold (2010); Carruthers (2014); Howes (2021). The miniature and borders are thought to have been executed by an English artist who was either trained in France or by a French artist in England [see Scott (2000)]. According to Scott (2000), the same artist worked on the decoration of at least three other extant manuscripts: Olim Longleat, Longleat House, MS 24 London, British Library, Royal MS 8 G III Oxford, Bodleian Library MS Auct. In a garden or animal enclosure, the infant Jesus nimbed and rayed in the centre of the scene flanked by Mary nimbed and Joseph. A ray of light falls from the sky and touches the head of the infant Jesus. Joseph holds a candle and shelters the flame with his cloak. Two shepherds approach in the distance. Folio 52v: Tierce of the Virgin. Adoration of the magi. In a garden or animal enclosure with building in right background and landscape scenery in left background. Mary nimbed and seated on right of scene holds the nimbed infant Jesus. Folio 60v: Compline of the Virgin. The Coronation of Mary. Interior scene with tiled floor and chequered walls. Mary nimbed kneels in left of scene before Jesus nimbed and throned on right of scene holding an orb and raising his right hand in benediction. Jesus nimbed and seated on a rainbow depicted in black and gold with his feet resting on a golden orb. On earth below Mary and John the Evangelist, both nimbed, kneel facing one another. Three heads emerge from graves in the earth. Folio 81v: Office of the Dead. Interior scene. At the end of the Dirrection of a Mannys Life (), The Charter of the Abbey of the Holy Ghost () and the Augustine excerpt () one sees the same practice of filling the end of a line of prose with a distinctive decorative ‘AMEN’. In each instance, this sequence is identical, consisting of each letter capitalised and separated by a decorative marking made up of a tilde stroke intersected by one or two vertical lines. The fact that this distinctive trait is present at the end of the first excerpt may evidence the fact that the same scribe copied the now largely lost first text as part of the surviving manuscript segment as opposed to repurposing a half-used quire to commence this compilation work. This practice is in contrast to the purely decorative line-filling that appears on .

The manuscript contains thirteen half-page miniatures in colours on gold-patterned grounds and inside architectural (Gothic pinnacled canopies) frames: twelve show scenes from the Life of David at the liturgical divisions of the Psalter, and one marks the begining of the Seven Penitential Psalms. The miniatures were painted by a group of artists who produced several psalters and books of hours for the Bohun family. Among this group was the Augustinian friar John de Teye (doc. 1361-1384), who is responsible for the opening miniature in this mansucript (f. 1r). The other paintings were done by a close associate who worked with him on most of Teye's other surviving Bohun manuscripts (see Sandler, Illuminators and Patrons (2014), p. 237). The miniatures show the following scenes: Miniature no. 1 at Psalm 1 ( Beatus vir) on f. 1r: David with raised club threatens a bear devouring one of his sheep (left). David about to sling a stone at a lion seizing a sheep (right). The two scnes are separated by a river with an angel with folded legs hovering above.Miniature no. 2 at Psalm 26 ( Dominus illuminatio mea) on f. 29r: David leading a procession of armed men, carrying Goliath's head and lance, and meeting a company of ladies with musical instruments.Miniature no. 3 at Psalm 38 ( Dixi custodiam) on f. 46r: David fleeing the soldiers of Saul (left). Almost every chapter in the volume begins with a historiated or decorative initial typically 4-6 lines high set within a square or rectangular frame with gold details and a spray border extending into the adjacent margin(s). The majority of these decorative initials present a literal depiction of the subject of the chapter, but some offer more abstract scenes or occasionally add or remove elements relative to the description of the chapter given in the rubric. The image cycle in CUL MS Ii.5.11 is of wider interest because of its similarities to other manuscript copies of the Regime du corps; the Binski and Zutshi Western Illuminated Manuscripts catalogue refers to similarities between the image cycle in this manuscript and the image cycle in the . A dissertation by Luís Miguel Campos Ribeiro 'Picturing Medieval Health: artistic production and visual discourse in Le Régime du corps of the Ajuda library (Cod 52-XIII-26)' (Lisbon, 2016) discusses CUL MS Ii.5.11 in relation to a similar cycle of images in New York, Morgan Library, MS M.165 , and Jennifer Borland has drawn attention to the similarities of the image cycle in these manuscripts and also Lisbon, Biblioteca Nacional de Portugal, MS Ajuda 52-XIII-26. Gold, blue and purple bar borders by two artists, extending from illuminated initials into vines with blue, purple, rose and orange leaves, gold discs, pen sprays and tendrils in one- or three-sided borders. Short sprays with gold discs, blue and purple leaves, extending from gold initials. Further fragments survive on stubs of folios whose initials have been cut out (e.g. ff. 193r, 277r, 381r). 'The style of the surviving borders is archaic and reminiscent of English border decoration at the beginning of the fifteenth century, although the large motifs in the infilling of the accompanying initials is more appropriate to a later date.' (Parkes and Beadle (1979-80), vol. 3, p. 60).

The manuscript contains two sketches drawn in red ink in the lower margins of ff. and . The first sketch illustrates lines 12 to 16 of f. , corresponding to Histories, Book II, 13, 7. It consists of a map representing the city of Athens on the left, the harbour of Phalerum on the right, and the Phaleric walls joining the two. The scribe also provided the drawing with some informative inscriptions using words directly borrowed from the text of Thucydides. Those include indications of distances in Greek numerals and of the guarded (φυλαττόμενον) and unguarded areas (ἀφύλακτον) on the map. Although the second sketch is found on f. , it illustrates lines 2 to 8 of f. , which corresponds to Histories, Book II, 15, 4. It shows the city walls of Plataea reinforced by a wooden structure made to ensure the protection of the city from the siege of the Lacedaemonians. Although the sketch was originally accompanied by three inscriptions, the one located below the sketch is now lost to trimming. The two other ones are Πλαταία (“Plataea”), which is written within the top circle representing the city of Plataea, and ξύλινον τεῖχος (“wooden wall”), located on the right side of the sketch.
